title: Ranges, Game Theory and Solvers
intro: Strong players don't ask what one opponent's hand is; they ask what range of hands it could be, and what their own range looks like to the opponent. This page covers range thinking, the game theory behind balanced strategies (often called GTO, game-theory optimal), two small toy games that show where bluffing frequencies come from, and how solver programs compute strategies for the full game.

blocks.text: Thinking in ranges

A range is every hand a player could hold in a spot, each with a weight for how likely they are to hold it there. Ranges narrow with every action: a player who opens under the gun, calls a 3-bet and then check-calls a flop has a much narrower and more particular range than one who opened. Hand reading is tracking that narrowing (see #/poker/probability for the counting).

Your own range matters just as much. If you bet only your strong hands, an observant opponent folds whenever you bet; if you check only your weak hands, they bet whenever you check. Choosing an action with the whole range in mind (what would I do here with each hand I could have?) is what makes a strategy hard to exploit. A range that mixes value hands and bluffs in the right proportion, and strong hands into its checks, is called balanced.

blocks.alt: Four horizontal bars, each running from weakest hands on the left to the strongest on the right, with the hands in the range shaded blue. Polarised: the strongest fifth and the weakest fifth are shaded, with nothing in the middle. Linear: everything from just below the middle up to the strongest. Condensed: only a middle band. Capped: everything from the weakest up to about two thirds, with the strongest hands missing.
blocks.caption: Four shapes a range can take. Each action a player takes reveals something about the shape of their range.

items: Polarised: very strong hands and bluffs, with few medium hands. Suits large bets, because a big bet gets paid by the hands it beats and folds out the hands that beat the bluffs.
Linear (merged): the strongest hands down to some cut-off. Suits smaller bets that get called by a wide range of slightly worse hands.
Condensed: mostly medium-strength hands, such as the range of a player who just calls a bet. A condensed range struggles against big bets.
Capped: a range that can't hold the strongest hands, because with them the player would have raised earlier. Capped ranges invite pressure.

blocks.text: Range advantage and nut advantage

On any board, compare the two ranges. Range advantage (equity advantage) is having more equity on average across the whole range. Nut advantage is having more of the very strongest hands. They are not the same: on 7 6 5, the preflop raiser's range of high cards and big pairs may still be close in overall equity, but the big blind, who defended with 98s, 43s, 76s and 55, holds far more of the straights, sets and two pairs. A player with the range advantage tends to bet often and small; a player with the nut advantage can bet big, including overbets, because the opponent can't have enough strong hands to resist.
Nash equilibrium and GTO

A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies, one per player, in which no player can gain by changing only their own (see #/game-theory/nash-equilibrium). In two-player zero-sum games such as heads-up poker an equilibrium strategy has a guarantee: it does at least as well as the value of the game against any opponent strategy at all, so it can't lose in expectation from a symmetric position (like playing both seats in turn). Poker players call such a strategy game-theory optimal (GTO). With three or more players that guarantee no longer holds, but equilibrium-like strategies still play very well in practice.

items: A GTO strategy is unexploitable, not maximally profitable. Against a player with clear mistakes, an exploitative strategy that targets them wins more, at the price of being exploitable in turn.

Exploitability measures how much a perfect counter-strategy would win against a strategy. An equilibrium has zero; solvers report how close their output is, often as a fraction of a percent of the pot.

Mixed strategies: an equilibrium often plays the same hand in more than one way, say betting it 60% of the time and checking 40%, because both actions have the same EV. A player can mix with a randomiser such as the second hand of a watch.

The indifference principle: at equilibrium, a player mixes between two actions only when they have equal EV. Opponents' frequencies are set to make each mixing hand indifferent. That is the source of the bluffing and calling frequencies below.

blocks.text: Toy game 1: the polarised river

The simplest model of river betting (the clairvoyant game in Chen and Ankenman). On the river the pot is $p$. The bettor holds either the nuts or nothing; the caller holds a bluff-catcher, a hand that beats every bluff and loses to every value hand. The bettor bets $b$. The caller is indifferent to calling when the share of bluffs in the betting range equals the pot odds:

blocks.caption: A pot-sized bet gives one bluff for every two value bets; a half-pot bet one for every three.

blocks.text: The bettor's bluffs are indifferent when the caller continues with the minimum defence frequency $p/(p+b)$ of #/poker/pot-odds-and-ev. Bigger bets mean more bluffs for each value hand and fewer calls. At equilibrium the bluffs earn exactly what checking would (nothing), but they are what gets the value bets paid.
Toy game 2: the AKQ game

A three-card deck holds an ace, a king and a queen. Each player antes 1 and gets one card. The first player must check; the second may bet 1 into the pot of 2 or check; facing a bet the first player calls or folds. The best card wins at showdown. The equilibrium:

items: The second player always bets an ace for value, never bets a king (it can only be called by the ace) and bluffs with a queen one time in three.
The first player always calls with an ace, always folds a queen and calls with a king one time in three.

Check the indifferences: when the first player holds the king, a bet comes from the ace with weight 1/2 and from a bluffing queen with weight $\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3}$, so a quarter of bets are bluffs, the same $b/(p+2b) = 1/(2+2) = 1/4$ as above. A call wins 3 (the pot plus the bet) a quarter of the time and loses 1 three quarters of the time: zero EV, so the king is indifferent.

When the second player holds the queen, the opponent holds an ace or a king equally often and calls with $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3}$, which is exactly the MDF $p/(p+b) = 2/3$; a bluff wins 2 a third of the time and loses 1 two thirds of the time, zero EV.

blocks.text: Real poker is enormously larger, but the same logic runs through it: the bets are made with a mix of strong hands and bluffs in proportion to the bet size, and the defence calls with enough bluff-catchers to make the bluffs break even.
Choosing bluffs and bluff-catchers

At equilibrium, which hands bluff and which call is decided largely by card removal (see #/poker/probability). The best bluffs block the opponent's calling hands and unblock their folds: on a river where a flush came in, a hand holding the lone ace of that suit (with no flush itself) makes it less likely that the opponent holds the nut flush. That makes it a prime bluff when you bet, and a better bluff-catcher when you face a bet. A missed straight draw holding cards the opponent would call with is a good bluff for the same reason. These effects are small per hand but decide which hands sit right on the boundary.
Equity realization

Equity assumes every hand gets to showdown with no more betting. In practice, hands out of position or with little playability get bet off their equity and realise less of it; hands in position, suited hands and connected hands realise more. Equity realization (EQR) is the ratio of what a hand actually wins to its raw equity share of the pot. A rough model for a call is: expected share of the pot $\approx$ equity $\times$ EQR. An offsuit hand in the big blind may realise only 70 to 80% of its equity; a suited connector on the button can realise more than 100%, because it wins big pots when it hits and folds cheaply when it misses.
Solvers

A solver computes an approximate equilibrium for a spot the user defines: the starting ranges, the board, the stack depths and a small menu of bet sizes for each street (allowing every possible size would make the game too big). Most use counterfactual regret minimisation (CFR, Zinkevich and others, 2007): the program plays the game against itself millions of times, and after each pass it shifts its strategy at every decision towards the actions it regrets not having taken more. In two-player zero-sum games the average strategy converges to a Nash equilibrium. Commercial solvers such as PioSOLVER and GTO Wizard work this way; research programs such as Libratus and Pluribus added methods for solving parts of the game in real time during play.

items: A solution is only as good as its inputs: the wrong starting ranges or bet sizes give a precise answer to the wrong question.
Abstraction: grouping similar hands or bet sizes into one, to make a game small enough to solve.

Node locking: fixing an opponent's strategy at one decision (say, making them fold too much to river bets) and letting the solver compute the best response. It is the bridge from GTO study to exploitative play.
Preflop solutions for six-handed games need simplifications, since a full equilibrium for three or more players is not guaranteed to be unexploitable and is very costly to compute.
Most players use solver output to learn principles (which boards to bet small, when to overbet, how often to defend) rather than memorising frequencies.

blocks.text: Using a solver's ideas against weaker players is not the same as copying its frequencies. GTO is the baseline that can't be beaten; profit against real opponents comes from noticing where they differ from it and adjusting.

blocks.title: Bluffs for an overbet
blocks.text: On the river you bet 1.5 times the pot with a polarised range. To make a bluff-catcher indifferent, what share of your betting range should be bluffs? How often must the opponent continue?
blocks.hint: Use bluffs over range $= b/(p + 2b)$ and MDF $= p/(p+b)$ with $b = 1.5p$.
solution: Bluff share $= 1.5 / (1 + 3) = 37.5\%$: three bluffs for every five value bets.
blocks.answer: 37.5% bluffs; they must continue 40% of the time

blocks.title: The AKQ game's value
blocks.text: In the AKQ game above, why does the second player never bet a king?
blocks.hint: Ask which hands call a bet and which fold.
solution: The first player calls with an ace and folds a queen. A bet with a king is called only by the hand that beats it and folds out only the hand it already beats.

So betting a king can only lose money compared with checking, which wins against the queen at showdown and loses to the ace. A bet that worse hands never call and better hands never fold is never a value bet or a bluff.
blocks.answer: a bet with the king is only called by better hands and only folds worse ones
